title: Earth, cry, and the witness in heaven
english: … the hills, as if to say: you do not know the things before creation.

“Earth, do not cover over the blood of my flesh, and let there be no place for my cry. And now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and the one who shares my knowledge is on high” (Job 16:18-19). At a loss, he speaks to the earth, and calling it to sympathy he says words that are spoken as a wish. He says: Do not keep silent, O earth, about what has befallen me, and do not help to hide the blood unjustly poured from my flesh through my sores. Let it not stand still in one place and be hidden, and let my laments not pass into forgetfulness. Rather, he says, let many be built up through my trials. Or: let the earth not hide my blood but call God out to vengeance, with the very discharges of my body as its witnesses. And may the air not hold back my cry, but may the force of my voice reach to heaven, so that God, standing up as avenger of the evils being done and punishing those responsible, may in this way at least show all people that my life has been blameless. The words “Behold, my witness is in heaven” belong to a most pure conscience.

“Only know that the Lord has done this to me” (Job 19:3). He brings them down to fear, as if to say: Do not trample on me like this in my suffering, or you too may fall into the same things, since you have the same nature. “Yes, in truth I have gone astray, and a deceiver lodges with me, so that I speak words I ought not; my words go astray and are out of season. But let it be that you magnify yourselves against me and leap on me with reproach” (Job 19:4-5). Let it be granted, he says, for argument's sake, that I have gone astray. “A deceiver lodges with me”: the deceiver is the devil. What harm, he says, comes to you from this? What need is there to judge me ungodly and to trample on a sufferer? You ought to pardon a man who speaks under pain. Even if I had done such things as I ought not, should you then have reproached me like this? And I, he says, who have long cared for godliness, ought now to have the confidence that comes from works. I have not done that, yet I am judged a deceiver.

He adds here too: “Know then that it is the Lord who has troubled me; he has raised his stronghold against me. Behold, I laugh at reproach; I will not speak. I will cry out, and there is no judgement anywhere” (Job 19:6-7). Consider, he says: I am not grieved without cause, hemmed in by my troubles as by a wall. I tell you truly, he says, how things stand with me, and you do not accept my words. “At reproach” is said to name the facts. “I will not speak” means: because you contradict me, I seem to have said nothing. And if I cry to God to bring my case into the open before all, I do not obtain my plea. No one hears, no one judges, I see no one, I have nowhere to go. Ought not these things to move pity? So leave off accusing me so recklessly, or God may bring you to judgement to exact from you the penalty for senseless rashness. For God, he says, does not leave such things unpunished. For it will happen, he says, if he is moved against you, that your conceit of knowing the good and your carelessness about what lies ahead will prove to have been of no profit to you.

Aquila and Symmachus: “What do you say? That I suffer these things because I am in wickedness? Then you too ought to fear the same things.” You would have hurried then, he says, though the facts bear witness, to argue in words. So take hold of your words, so that not even the truth may vote you free of account. The Hebrew at any rate also has “a sin of word”.

“May the lesser destroy his sons, and may his hands kindle pains” (Job 20:10). And those who were formerly beneath them, he says, will get the better of the lawless man's children. “Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited up; an angel will drag him out of his house” (Job 20:15). The ungodly man does everything so as to take what belongs to others, and all that he does looks to this aim; but when he seems to be master of everything, then he will see it carried over to others. “Like tough gristle that cannot be chewed or swallowed” (Job 20:18). The words and doctrines of the ungodly are tough and [unpalatable], for the things done against God have nothing sweet in them. “When he seems already to be filled, he will be afflicted, and every distress will come upon him” (Job 20:22). He says this: because of the cause, what was acquired is lost and is not handed on in his family. “May he send upon him the fury of wrath, may he rain pains upon him” (Job 20:23). That is: he will suffer terrible things from God and from heaven. He said this because Job, after saying that he had been struck by God, also spoke of being wronged by men; so he sets out to show that everything was brought on him through sin. “And stars in his dwellings …” (Job 20:25)

title: The Nature of Wickedness and the Office of the Bishop
english: “… may walk about” (Job 20:25). … For they are in ignorance: they cast the light away from themselves, they to whom he said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

“An unkindled fire will devour him” (Job 20:26). In the hidden sense, the unkindled fire is either the fire of conscience, or else the fire laid up in the places of punishment to come. And he will be consumed as by fire, he says, meaning: he is not even thought worthy of burial.

“This is the portion of an ungodly man from the Lord, and the possession of his goods from the Bishop” (Job 20:29). It is the portion by which divine justice is set in motion against him. Whether he is the man from the circumcision who has been ungodly toward God because of Christ, or the man of strange opinions, or ungodly in any way whatever, the portion here declared is his. Learn who is here named Bishop: God is called Bishop, and the bishops, the good and noble ones, make it their ambition in every way to bear his image. And just as one who copies a royal image is honored for copying it well, and honored also for having adorned it, so blessed is the bishop who has understood the true Bishop, and emulates him, and becomes as God among men; or the one who has as his bishop him who makes him truly a bishop in Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory and the might to the ages of ages. Amen.

“And their children play, taking up psaltery and lyre, and they rejoice at the sound of a psalm” (Job 21:11-12). See, their foolish children too are playing among themselves. For they recite psalms of Valentinus and odes of Basilides, and they utter such things, rejoicing at the sound of a psalm.

“Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?” Let us see what Eliphaz says to the righteous man: “Is it not,” and so on … When Job had said this, Eliphaz too falls in with the argument and says: I too know that the reasons why one man, though ungodly, prospers and another is punished are known to God, who alone is wise. And I know this as well: God, as you yourself said, is the giver of good things, but wickedness deals out the punishments. The teaching is sound … Knowledge is the comprehensive contemplation of things that always hold the same way; understanding is discernment.

“Is not your wickedness great, and your sins without number?” (Job 22:5). With reason, then, I say that you have not simply become unjust, since you suffer such things as none of the wicked suffer, but that you were born in these things; plainly, you have had more wickedness than the others among the wicked. Wickedness is a bad state in the soul, as of grief or of anger, and unseemly desire; sin is its activity. That is why he named wickedness first and then sin, calling the one great and the others numberless. I see a great many sinners, and none of them has fallen into such evils as you have. For it is likely that these things have come upon you because of your numberless sins and the multitude of your stumbles.

“You took pledges from your brothers for nothing, and stripped the naked of their clothing” (Job 22:6). Let us take heed, we who lend at interest, that we never take pledges for nothing. The words are useful: in this respect it is reasonable to speak truly of sins, of things done blameworthily among men. Eliphaz suspects this of Job because he knew he was rich, and he suspected that he had grown rich from some such sources. So he says, “You took pledges for nothing,” that is, when nothing was owed you. If I lent, and, not trusting the borrower, took a pledge worth what I lent, I took a pledge, but not for nothing. But if I bring a false charge against a man, saying that he owes me when he cannot repay, and I demand and take, then I take a pledge for nothing.

He presses further again, supposing that another sin of his had taken place. One may sometimes take garments, not from the naked, but from a rich man who has many other clothes laid by, and take, say, three; from those many I took clothing there. The naked man's case is one thing, the rich man's another. But if someone has one tunic, and on the pretext of demanding what is mine I strip that tunic off him, without pity for that naked man, I have taken away the clothing of the naked.

Many such things happen among us when we lend, when we go after debtors. Often our debtor is poor beyond measure and cannot repay; and we shut up our hearts and become pitiless and cruel, not seeing that he feeds a wife and children and barely feeds himself on the few obols he earns. We demand payment bitterly, sometimes even when we have more than enough laid by. Such things happen in bitter demands for payment; sometimes …

title: Accountability for Inaction
english: … someone has just that one morsel, and though he has no whole loaf, we take it from him, saying: But you owe. So he says these things in charging Job with having stripped the naked of their clothing.

“You did not give water to the thirsty to drink, but deprived the hungry of a morsel. You admired the face of some, and you lodged those who are on the ground. You sent widows away empty, and you ill-treated orphans” (Job 22:7-9). So not only doing wrong but also failing to do good is liable to account. And he points out how far we ought to extend our kindness, since not giving drink to the thirsty is liable to account. Just as we receive a reward for the cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42), so he condemns Job for great harshness, as one who did not give even water, a kindness that costs nothing, and, the greater evil, to someone thirsty.

“But you deprived the hungry of a morsel.” Why do I say, he says, that you did not give to the one in need, when you even took from the hungry man the small comfort of bread? For by “morsel” he means a piece of bread, as it stands also in Ruth: “Dip your morsel in the vinegar” (Ruth 2:14).

“You admired the face of some.” That is, you also gave your judgements not justly, nor without passion, but to please men, for you became a respecter of persons. In judging, you raised some up and brought others low, doing violence to the lowly and admiring and honoring those in power.

“And you lodged those who are on the ground.” Some of the copies have “you laid to sleep” instead of “you lodged,” meaning: you took away even the very bedding of the poor, so that they had to sleep on the floor, with nothing spread beneath them … “You sent widows away.” Either you stripped them of what they had, or rather, when they came to you asking for alms, you gave them nothing but sent them away without anything from you … “You ill-treated orphans.” To ill-treat orphans and the helpless is the mark of the utmost wickedness. For one must ill-treat no one, but above all one must spare orphans, since God commanded us to fight for helpless souls. More than other people, the poor, widows and orphans need help.

“And the counsel of the ungodly is far from him. The righteous saw it and laughed” (Job 22:18-19). What the ungodly plan is far from God. The righteous, seeing the counsel of the ungodly, laughed them to scorn.

“Receive a declaration from his mouth, and take up his words in your heart” (Job 22:22). I was asking myself what “declaration” means, and I found that in another edition, that of Symmachus, “confession” stands in its place, and in Aquila “law.” So according to the one he says: Confess your sins, and be taught by God the manner of the declaration. According to the other: Receive law from God, and take his words into your heart. If you are righteous and worthy, let God dictate to you, and receive divine words in your heart, as Jeremiah later heard: “Behold, I have given my words into your mouth” (Jeremiah 1:9). Or by “declaration” he means confession, urging the righteous man to repentance. Or he is saying: Change your way of life and take up the divine laws. Or: Declare the sins you have committed, and from now on keep the words of God. The starting points for this double sense I took from there, from the word “declaration.”
“You will lay it on a mound in the rock, and like the rock of the torrent of Sophir” (Job 22:24). You will throw it to the ground and, as it were, ill-treat it.

“And indeed I know that the reproof comes from my own hand, and his hand has become heavy upon my groaning” (Job 23:2). That is: I carry my accuser about with me; the reproof, the proof of my evils, I have from my own house. I know, he says, that it is from what is at hand, that is, from the blow, and not from what I have done, that you think to bring your reproofs; for God has laid himself on me heavily, so that I groan. I know, he says, that men's judgements come to them from their deeds; but the reproof has been laid on me beyond my strength, that is, apart from anything I have done.

“And he will come against me in great strength; then he will not use threats against me” (Job 23:6). For even if he deals with me in great strength and threat, still I know that truth is with him. “For truth and reproof are from him; and may he bring my judgement to its end” (Job 23:7). This was his prayer; this is what he means: that an end be set to my troubles. Then, he says: I wished these things to happen, so that I might die, not as though he were now about to judge. Among the Hebrews, “end” and “victory” are expressed by one word.
“For he already knows my way” (Job 23:10). He knows my way, he says, and that I have always been eager to obey …
